name: class
desc: Declares a type. The class is the blueprint, each object made from it is an instance with its own field values.
body: One file can hold several classes, but only one of them may be `public`, and its name must match the file name. A class with no access modifier is visible only inside its package. Fields belong to each object; a `static` field belongs to the class. Keep the fields `private` and expose behaviour through methods so the object decides what is legal.

name: new
desc: Allocates one object on the heap, fills fields with default values, runs a constructor, and returns a reference.
body: `new` returns a reference, not the object itself. Java passes that reference by value into methods, so a method can change the object's fields but cannot make your variable point at something else. Comparing two references with `==` asks whether they point at the same object, not whether their contents match.

name: instance field
desc: A variable stored in every object. A final field is assigned once and cannot change afterwards.
body: A field declared `final` can be assigned where it is declared or in every constructor, nowhere else. That makes it a safe default for identity values such as an id or a name. Without `final`, every public setter is a door into the state, so add one only when the value really has to change.

name: instance method
desc: Behaviour that runs with a this reference to the object it was called on, so it can read and write that object's fields.
body: The signature is the name plus the parameter types. The return type is not part of it, so two methods cannot differ only by return type. A method with no parameters still has access to `this`, which is why `isLuxury()` can read `stars` without receiving the object as an argument.

name: constructor
desc: Runs once per object, after the fields get their default values. It has no return type and its job is to leave the object valid.
body: If you write no constructor, the compiler adds a no argument one. The moment you write any constructor, that free one is gone, so `new Hotel()` stops compiling. Validate inside the constructor: an object that throws there never reaches the rest of the program. A constructor has no return type, not even `void`.

name: this
desc: Refers to the current object. Needed when a parameter has the same name as a field, and as this(...) to chain constructors.
body: `this(...)` must be the first statement of a constructor, so a constructor either chains to another one or calls `super(...)`, never both. After a chain, the compiler still inserts one `super()` call at the top of the chain. Forgetting `this` in an assignment such as `name = name` assigns the parameter to itself and leaves the field `null`.

name: constructor chaining
desc: Calls another constructor of the same class. Keeps validation in one place instead of copying it into every overload.
body: Chain toward the constructor with the most parameters and let it do all the work. Every shorter constructor becomes one line, and a new validation rule is added once. The chain must be a straight line; a cycle of `this(...)` calls does not compile.

name: private fields
desc: Hides state behind the class boundary. Other classes can only change it through the methods you provide.
body: Encapsulation keeps one rule in one place. When `stars` can only be written by `setStars`, no future class can store `9` without passing the check. A class with public fields cannot make that promise.

name: getter
desc: Returns a field or a value derived from it. Booleans use the isField() form. Records use the bare component name.
body: Do not write a getter for every field by reflex. A getter on a mutable collection hands out the internal list, which lets a caller add items without validation; return `List.copyOf(...)` in that case. A field that never changes after construction should be `final` with a getter and no setter, so the compiler enforces the rule.

name: setter
desc: The single door into a mutable field. It validates before assigning, so no caller can store an invalid value.
body: The constructor should call the setters, not assign the fields directly, otherwise the object is validated on one path and not on the other. A setter that only assigns with no check is usually a sign the field should have been `final`. Validation that depends on several fields at once belongs in a method such as `validate()`, not in one setter.

name: access modifiers
desc: Control who can see a class, field, constructor, or method. Start private and widen only when a caller needs it.
body: A top level class can only be `public` or package-private. `protected` means the same package plus subclasses, which is wider than most beginners expect. Narrowing visibility in an override is a compile error, so a `public` parent method must stay `public` in every subclass.

name: static field
desc: One value shared by the class, not one per object. Initialised once when the class is loaded.
body: Reach a static field through the class name, `Hotel.created`, not through an object. `static final` on an object type freezes the reference, not the object: a `static final List` can still be added to. Constants use `static final` and upper case names. Static mutable state is global state, so tests that run in one JVM share it.

name: static method
desc: Belongs to the class. It has no this, so it cannot read instance fields or call instance methods directly.
body: `Math.max`, `Integer.parseInt`, and `List.of` are all static. A static method is the right home for a pure calculation that needs no object state. A static method cannot be overridden; a subclass can only declare a new one with the same name, and the variable type decides which runs.

name: static factory method
syntax: static Type of(parameters) { return new Type(...); }
desc: A named static method that builds objects. It can validate first, cache instances, and return a subtype.
body: A factory can have a readable name (`of`, `from`, `valueOf`, `parse`), while a constructor always carries the class name. It can also return a cached instance or a subclass. The cost is that a private constructor blocks inheritance from outside, which is often the point.

name: extends
desc: Inherits the parent's non-private fields and methods, and adds or replaces behaviour. Java allows one parent class only.
body: Private members are not inherited, and a constructor is never inherited. Initialisation order is: parent field defaults, parent constructor, child field defaults, child constructor. A subclass should pass the is-a test; when it only wants the code, composition with a field is the safer design.

name: super
desc: Calls a parent constructor, or the parent version of an overridden method. There is only one level up.
body: `super(...)` must be the first statement of the constructor. `super.method()` can appear anywhere and is the usual way to keep the parent's part of a description or calculation. `super.super.method()` does not exist in Java.

name: @Override
desc: Marks a method that replaces an inherited one. The compiler checks the signature, so a typo fails the build instead of adding a new method.
body: Overriding needs the same name and the same parameter types, at least the same visibility, and a return type that is the same or a subtype. `final`, `static`, and `private` methods cannot be overridden. A static method with the same signature is hidden, and the variable type chooses which one runs. Overloads are chosen at compile time; overrides at runtime.

name: abstract class
syntax: abstract class Name { abstract ReturnType m(); }
desc: A class that cannot be instantiated. It holds shared state and forces subclasses to provide the missing methods.
body: An abstract class can have fields, constructors, and concrete methods; an interface cannot hold instance state. An abstract method has no body and cannot be `private`, `static`, or `final`. A subclass that misses one abstract method must itself be declared abstract. The `final` template method here fixes the calculation order while subclasses supply the numbers.

name: interface
desc: A contract of methods. A class can implement many interfaces, so one object can be used through several unrelated types.
body: Interface methods are implicitly `public abstract`, and a field in an interface is implicitly `public static final`. The implementing method must be `public`, because the contract is public even when the keyword is absent. Cast between interfaces only when you know the object implements both; a blind cast throws `ClassCastException`.

name: default method
desc: A method with a body inside an interface. Implementing classes inherit it and may override it.
body: A default method lets you add behaviour to an interface without breaking every class that implements it. If two interfaces provide the same default method, the class must override it and pick one with `InterfaceName.super.method()`. An interface can also declare `static` methods, called on the interface name, and private helper methods used only inside the interface.

name: dynamic dispatch
desc: The method that runs is chosen from the object's real class at runtime, not from the variable's declared type.
body: A parent typed variable can hold any subclass object. The compiler checks only that the method exists on the variable type; the JVM picks the overriding version from the object. This is why a loop over a list of the parent type needs no `if` on the concrete class. Overloads behave the opposite way: they are resolved at compile time from the declared type.

name: instanceof pattern
desc: Tests the runtime type and, when it matches, binds the cast object to a new variable in one step.
body: The pattern variable is in scope only where the test is true, so there is no cast to forget. `instanceof null` is always false, which makes the check safe before any cast. Use it to reach subclass specific state; do not use it to replace dispatch with a chain of type tests, because every new subclass then needs an edit in that chain.

name: record
desc: A compact immutable data class. The compiler writes the private final fields, constructor, accessors, toString, equals, and hashCode.
body: A record is implicitly `final` and extends `java.lang.Record`, so it cannot extend another class. It can implement interfaces and declare extra methods, but not extra instance fields. Accessors are named after the components, `name()` rather than `getName()`. Use a record for a parsed row, a request, or a result that never changes.

name: compact constructor
desc: A constructor without a parameter list that validates or normalises the components before the fields are assigned.
body: In the compact form you write only the body, and the compiler assigns each field from the matching parameter at the end. Reassigning a parameter changes what gets stored, which is the clean place to trim or default a value. A record can also declare a normal constructor, but then it must delegate to the canonical one with `this(...)`.

name: toString
desc: Returns the text used by println, logging, and string concatenation. Without it the output is a class name and a hash.
body: `println` calls `String.valueOf(object)`, which calls `toString()` unless the reference is null. Concatenation does the same. Put the identifying fields in the output, not every field: a log line that dumps a whole object graph is unreadable. Records generate a readable `toString` already, so override only when the default is too noisy.

name: equals and hashCode
syntax: @Override public boolean equals(Object o); @Override public int hashCode();
desc: Define value equality and a matching hash. Override both together or the object misbehaves inside HashSet and HashMap.
body: The contract: equal objects must have equal hash codes, and `equals` must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, and consistent. Comparing with `instanceof` allows subclasses to compare equal; `getClass()` is stricter. Records generate both methods, so a record in a `HashSet` deduplicates with no code. Never use a mutable field in `hashCode` while the object sits in a hash based collection.
